---
title: Reward models
jupyter: python3
---

A reward model gives one number per item, and it learns from pairs: two items
and which one a person preferred. Laplace gives each reward an error bar. Our
items are points in the cube [-2, 2]³, and a hidden utility of the first two
coordinates decides the labels.

::: {.callout-note title="Plugin"}
This page uses the
[`laplacekit-reward`](https://github.com/laplacekit/laplacekit/tree/main/plugins/reward)
plugin. Install it with

```bash
pip install "laplacekit[reward]"
```
:::

::: {#3063d58d .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch import nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset

import laplacekit as lk

torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
torch.manual_seed(2027)


def utility(x):
    return torch.sin(2 * x[:, 0]) + x[:, 1]


first, second = 4 * torch.rand(300, 3) - 2, 4 * torch.rand(300, 3) - 2
p_first = torch.sigmoid(3 * (utility(first) - utility(second)))
label = (
    torch.rand(300) > p_first
).long()  # the index of the preferred item, 0 = first
```
:::


The network scores one item. `lk.reward.pairwise` turns it into a model that
scores both items of a pair, and Bradley–Terry is the cross-entropy over the
two rewards. The labels only see the difference of two rewards, so the data
can't pin down a shift of all of them. A bias in the last layer would be such
a shift, so we leave it out.

::: {#6e5be1bd .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 1, bias=False))
model = lk.reward.pairwise(net)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=1e-2, weight_decay=1e-2)

for _ in range(300):
    rewards = torch.cat([net(first), net(second)], -1)  # [300, 2]
    opt.zero_grad()
    F.cross_entropy(rewards, label).backward()
    opt.step()
```
:::


`lk.reward.prepare_pairs` turns the `(first, second, label)` rows of the
loader into batches of pairs, and `lk.reward.bradley_terry()` is the
likelihood.

::: {#e69aed18 .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(first, second, label), batch_size=100)
data = lk.data.from_loader(loader, prepare=lk.reward.prepare_pairs)

post = lk.laplace(model, data, likelihood=lk.reward.bradley_terry())
print(post)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
LaplacePosterior(
  subset         = last_layer {"2.weight": (1, 32)}
  hessian_approx = PerBlockCurvature({'*': DenseGGN()})
  curvature      = BlockDiag[Dense] (1 block, 32 parameters)
  prior          = Isotropic(prior_precision=0.819)
  likelihood     = Categorical()
  hyper_tuner    = MarginalLikelihood()
  n_data         = 300
)
```
:::
:::


On single items, `lk.predict_outputs` gives the reward with its variance. We move the
first coordinate from -4 to 4, past the data on both sides, and keep the
other two at zero.

::: {#d4d08d08 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
t = torch.linspace(-4.0, 4.0, 201)
items = torch.stack([t, torch.zeros_like(t), torch.zeros_like(t)], 1)

out = lk.predict_outputs(post, items)
reward = out.mean.squeeze()
std = out.cov.per_input().squeeze().sqrt()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.axvspan(-2, 2, color="0.93", label="data range")
ax.plot(t, utility(items), "k--", label="utility")
ax.plot(t, reward, label="reward")
ax.fill_between(
    t, reward - 2 * std, reward + 2 * std, alpha=0.3, label="± 2 std"
)
ax.set_xlabel("first coordinate")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

print(f"reward std: {float(std[100]):.3f} at 0, {float(std[-1]):.3f} at 4")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](reward_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=569 height=357}
:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
reward std: 0.527 at 0, 1.415 at 4
```
:::
:::


Inside the data range the reward roughly follows the shape of the utility.
Pairs say nothing about the level of the rewards, so the curve sits wherever
training left it. The reward's standard deviation is 0.527 at zero and grows
to 1.415 at 4, past the data.

On a `Pair`, `lk.predict` gives the preference probabilities.

::: {#fcebb64c .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
a = torch.tensor([[0.75, 0.0, 0.0]])
b = torch.tensor([[-0.75, 0.0, 0.0]])

probs = lk.predict(post, lk.reward.Pair(a, b)).probs.squeeze()

print(f"utility: a {float(utility(a)):.3f}, b {float(utility(b)):.3f}")
print(f"P(a wins) {float(probs[0]):.3f}, P(b wins) {float(probs[1]):.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
utility: a 0.997, b -0.997
P(a wins) 0.869, P(b wins) 0.131
```
:::
:::


The utilities are 0.997 and -0.997, so with the labels' factor of 3, the
true probability that `a` wins is σ(3 × 1.994) ≈ 0.997. The Laplace
predictive gives 0.869. It picks the same winner and is less sure.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The math"}
Bradley–Terry says that a person prefers item $a$ to item $b$ with

$$
  p(a \succ b) = \sigma\big(r(a) - r(b)\big) ,
$$

which is the softmax over the two rewards. Laplace puts a Gaussian on the
weights, and the linearized network turns it into a Gaussian over the two
rewards. Their difference $d = r(a) - r(b)$ is then Gaussian too, with mean
$\mu_d$ and variance $v_d = V_{aa} + V_{bb} - 2 V_{ab}$, and the probit
approximation gives

$$
  p(a \succ b \mid \mathcal{D}) \approx \sigma\Big(\frac{\mu_d}{\sqrt{1 + \frac{\pi}{8} v_d}}\Big) .
$$
:::
